A strain-wave reducer requires a flexspline (one of its three canonical members); the flexspline is the fatigue-life-limiting, hardest-to-manufacture part.
A strain-wave reducer requires a circular spline (rigid internal ring gear), the second of its three canonical members.
A strain-wave reducer requires a wave generator (elliptical cam plus deformable flex bearing), the third of its three canonical members.
The strain-wave reducer's joint output is carried by a thin-section cross-roller bearing (often integrated into the reducer/joint housing).
The reducer's bearings and flex bearing are made from high-cleanliness bearing steel; parented here (not under the flexspline) to keep the feedstock within the depth-4 render budget.
A planetary roller screw requires a precision multi-start threaded central shaft.
A planetary roller screw requires a set of profile-ground planetary rollers; roller grinding is the throughput-limiting step.
A planetary roller screw requires a coaxial internal-thread nut with integrated ring gears that time the rollers.
Planetary rollers are made from 52100-class high-cleanliness bearing steel (shared feedstock with the reducer bearings).
The micro hand actuator is driven by a coreless / hollow-cup micro motor (per the Optimus Gen-3 hollow-cup + lead-screw + tendon architecture).
The micro hand actuator uses a miniature lead/ball screw to convert motor rotation into the linear tendon pull.
The fingertip tactile array requires a tactile sensing element (MEMS, magnetic, or visuotactile transducer).
Coreless/slotless hand motors use NdFeB-class permanent magnets (shared rare-earth magnet dependency).
A Li-ion cell requires a cathode active material; high-nickel NMC dominates cell cost and energy.
A Li-ion cell requires an anode active material (graphite, increasingly Si-blended).
A Li-ion cell requires a microporous separator film; high-power separator is a recognized few-supplier chokepoint.
The battery management system requires an analog front-end / fuel-gauge IC to monitor and balance cells.
The frameless BLDC motor core is built from thin electrical (silicon) steel laminations.
The frameless BLDC motor stator is wound with insulated copper magnet wire.
The rare-earth magnet supply is produced from sintered NdFeB feedstock (with Dy/Tb for high-temperature coercivity); a China-concentrated upstream chokepoint.
A six-axis force/torque sensor requires a precision-machined elastic element whose strain encodes the load.
The elastic element requires strain transducers (foil gauges or silicon piezoresistors) wired into Wheatstone bridges.
The joint encoder commonly uses a magnetic encoder ASIC (Hall array) over a diametrically polarized magnet for compact absolute angle sensing.
Where higher resolution is needed (output-side / dual-encoder designs), the joint encoder uses an optical code disk and photodetector.
The lightweight skeleton frame uses structural aluminum alloy for primary members and brackets.
The lightweight skeleton frame uses die-cast magnesium alloy for the lightest structural housings.
The torso enclosure and joint mechanisms use PEEK / carbon-fiber-reinforced polymer for low-mass, high-specific-strength parts.
The joint inverter power stage requires a low-voltage power switching device (Si MOSFET or GaN FET).
The depth camera requires a CMOS image sensor plus a structured-light/ToF emitter (VCSEL/IR) as its front end.
IMU attitude sensing requires a six-axis MEMS inertial die (gyro + accelerometer).
The edge AI compute module requires an onboard inference SoC (the named compute chokepoint).
The edge AI compute module requires on-module LPDDR memory; the upstream DRAM/HBM chain is a documented boundary owned by the ai_compute_chain domain.
High-duty-cycle motor/joint thermal paths use a heat pipe or vapor chamber as a two-phase spreader (the high-duty-cycle option, not universal).
The compute heat spreader requires a thermal interface material between the die/source and the spreader.
